newsitem.title: USA: Du Pont jury enters fifth day of deliberations.
newsitem.headline: Du Pont jury enters fifth day of deliberations.

text.p: Jurors in the trial of accused murderer John du Pont began a fifth day of deliberations on Saturday with yet another legal explanation from the judge.

The jury, which is confronted with eight possible verdicts in the case, had asked Delaware County Court of Common Pleas Judge Patricia Jenkins to once more repeat the legal definition of first-degree murder -- an indication they may be narrowing the focus of drawn out deliberations.
This was the fifth time the murder definition was read to the jurors, including in the initial instructions.

But the focus of the jurors' questions has steadily narrowed, and Friday's request made no mention of third-degree murder and voluntary manslaughter charges the jurors asked about on previous occasions.
Du Pont, a millionaire chemicals heir, is charged with first- and third-degree murder as well as voluntary manslaughter in the Jan. 26, 1996 killing of Olympic champion wrestler David Schultz.
Du Pont's lawyers have conceded du Pont killed Schultz, but they are seeking a verdict of not guilty by reason of insanity, saying he was unaware of the wrongfulness of his acts.

In her instructions repeated Saturday, which were based on standard descriptions recognised by Pennsylvania law, Jenkins told the jurors that to find a verdict of first-degree murder, the prosecution must prove du Pont had a specific intent to kill and acted with malice.
Malice, in turn, required an intent to kill or cause serious harm, or an "extreme indifference to human life."
If du Pont killed Schultz from a mistaken belief that he was in imminent danger of death or serious injury, the only charge he could be conviced on would be voluntary manslaughter, she said.

"If reasonable doubt as to whether the defendant killed David Schultz out of an honest, good faith, ... belief that he was in imminent danger ... then the element of malice is not proven and you may not find the defendent guilty of murder," she said.
In addition to verdicts of not guilty or not guilty by reason of insanity, the jurors can render verdicts of guilty or guilty but mentally ill.
